title: More than users: How political parties shape the acceptance of electoral clientelism

selected_claim.evidence_location: Figure 2 and Online Appendix 2, in the Results section “Explaining the acceptance of clientelism.” Figure 2 presents the marginal effects; the appendix gives the regression models.
selected_claim.evidence_summary: In the OLS model with controls, more frequent interaction with party members between elections is associated with greater acceptance of electoral clientelism. The paper also estimates adjusted associations for other party-exposure measures, including party membership and trust in parties. These are observational survey estimates, not randomized effects.
selected_claim.x: Respondents’ reported frequency of interaction with members (including leaders) of the main political parties in their locality or area of residence between elections, measured on a five-point scale from “very little” to “very much.”
selected_claim.y: Acceptance of electoral clientelism, measured as a cumulative index of respondents’ acceptability ratings for vote buying, food or product offers, promises of preferential access to public services or goods, and job promises in exchange for votes.
selected_claim.target_population: Romanian adults represented by the nationwide survey sample (N = 4,313), conducted in January 2021.
selected_claim.adjustment_description: The full OLS specification adjusts for other party-related measures and the five stated control variables: importance of the 2020 local elections, education, age, household per-capita income, and area of residence.
covariates: Perceived activity of the main political parties in the respondent’s locality between elections
Perceived strength of the local PSD organization
Perceived strength of the local PNL organization
Perceived strength of the local USR organization
Perceived strength of the local AUR organization
Perceived strength of the local UDMR organization

article_review.evidence: In the OLS model with controls, more frequent interaction with party members between elections is associated with greater acceptance of electoral clientelism. The paper also estimates adjusted associations for other party-exposure measures, including party membership and trust in parties. These are observational survey estimates, not randomized effects.
article_review.evidence_location: Figure 2 and Online Appendix 2, in the Results section “Explaining the acceptance of clientelism.” Figure 2 presents the marginal effects; the appendix gives the regression models.
article_review.adjustment: The full OLS specification adjusts for other party-related measures and the five stated control variables: importance of the 2020 local elections, education, age, household per-capita income, and area of residence.

evidence_summary: The focal paper asks whether respondents’ reported frequency of interaction with members and leaders of political parties in their local area between elections is associated with acceptance of electoral clientelism. Its cumulative outcome covers acceptability of vote buying, material offers, preferential access to public goods or services, and job promises in exchange for votes. The described data are a nationwide Romanian adult survey (N=4,313) conducted in January 2021. The full OLS specification adjusts for other party-related measures and the stated controls: importance of the 2020 local elections, education, age, household per-capita income, and area of residence. No effect estimates or causal identification details beyond this adjustment description were supplied.
x_definition: Respondents’ frequency of interaction with members, including leaders, of political parties in their locality or area of residence between elections.
y_definition: Individual acceptance of electoral clientelism, including acceptability of vote buying and offers of goods, services, or jobs in exchange for votes.

confounders.reason: The main OLS specification directly controls for respondents’ age (c11), measured in six age categories. This adjusts for broad age and life-stage differences relevant to both party interaction and clientelism acceptance, though the categories may not capture finer-grained age or cohort differences.

No control-inventory entry covers civil-conflict participation or exposure, and none of the listed controls is a substantively reasonable proxy for it. Area of residence captures settlement size and local context, not exposure to organized armed conflict. The confounder therefore remains unaddressed in the focal specification.

No control-inventory entry covers consumer/product/service evaluation or a substantively reasonable proxy for it. The listed controls for education, income, age, residence, party activity, organizational strength, and membership do not measure this construct. c8 (trust in political parties) is an intervening variable and concerns political legitimacy rather than commercial product or service evaluation; it does not count as a control for this confounder.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the exposure was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the outcome was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

The full OLS specification directly controls for education (inventory entry c10) in the main specification. It measures the respondent’s highest completed degree on a five-category scale, matching the confounder rather than serving merely as a proxy. It may not capture educational quality, field of study, or all knowledge and skills, but those limitations do not change the status.

The control inventory contains no pre-treatment control or design feature that covers transient emotion or affect. The stated controls do not provide a reasonable proxy for a respondent’s situation-specific emotional state. c8, trust in political parties, is an intervening variable and would not count as adjustment for this confounder in any event.

No inventory entry directly controls empirical political or policy beliefs, or is a substantively reasonable proxy for them. c9 measures election importance or salience, not empirical belief; c10 measures education and political knowledge, not beliefs about politics or social conditions. c8 concerns trust in political parties, which is distinct from this candidate construct and has role intervening_variable, so it does not count as a control. The remaining party-organization, membership, income, age, and residence entries do not track these beliefs. Thus no entry handles this confounder in the main specification.

No main-specification pre-treatment control or design feature in the inventory directly measures family-of-origin conditions or provides a substantively reasonable proxy for them. Current education, age, income, party membership, organizational measures, and local residence do not reliably capture parental characteristics or childhood family resources and experiences. The reported alternative specifications address outcome distribution and missing-data sensitivity, not family background.

No control inventory entry covers marital or partnership status, household composition, family-member presence or kinship arrangement, or a substantively reasonable proxy for family structure. The model’s age, income, education and area-of-residence controls do not directly adjust for family structure; age is not an adequate proxy for respondents’ actual household or partnership arrangements. The paper does not otherwise establish a structural reason to remove this confounder.

The full OLS specification includes c12, household per-capita income, as a direct pre-treatment control for income/earnings. It appears in the main specification. It measures household economic resources, though it may not capture individual earnings, income instability, or shocks.

No inventory entry directly controls or reasonably proxies general information or communication exposure. c1 measures local party activity and opportunities for contact, not whether respondents encounter messages, media content, frames, or other communication environments; the remaining entries likewise do not measure this exposure. The specification therefore does not address this confounder.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the exposure was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

No main-specification pre-treatment control or design feature in the inventory measures or reasonably proxies interpersonal/social trust. c8 (trust in political parties) is trust-adjacent but concerns confidence in a political institution, not trust in other people; it is also classified as an intervening_variable, which cannot count as adjustment for a confounder. The other listed controls do not proxy interpersonal/social trust.

No inventory entry controls labor-force status or a substantively reasonable proxy for it. In particular, c12 (income) measures household economic resources, not whether a respondent is employed, unemployed, retired, or otherwise participating in paid work; c10 (education) and c11 (age) likewise do not identify labor-force status. The party-related entries do not measure respondents’ employment position.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the exposure was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

The main specification includes c13, area of residence, as a direct control for the respondent’s geographic residence. It is measured from village through large city and captures rural–urban and settlement-size differences relevant to this confounder. It may not capture exact neighborhood location, distance, or variation within each settlement category.

No inventory entry controls objective aggregate macroeconomic context. c12 controls respondents’ household income, which is not a proxy for aggregate conditions such as unemployment, inflation, or local economic shocks. c13 controls area of residence and local context, but not the economic conditions within that context; c1 concerns party activity rather than macroeconomic conditions. The candidate is therefore unaddressed.

The main specification includes c7, party membership, as an imperfect proxy for readiness to interact with party members: formal affiliation and party involvement can track that readiness for some respondents. It may not capture motivation among nonmembers, or readiness for other specific behaviors represented by this broad candidate group.

No control inventory entry covers aggregate national cultural norms or values. c13, area of residence, controls for rural–urban residence, settlement size, and local context; it does not control for national cultural variation. The other controls likewise do not adjust for national cultural context.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the outcome was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

No pre-treatment control or design feature in the inventory directly measures or reasonably proxies respondents’ perceived peer-group norms. The party activity, organizational strength, membership, election-importance, education, age, income, and residence entries do not capture those norms. c8, trust in political parties, is an intervening variable rather than a control and is not itself a measure of peer-group norms, so it does not address this confounder.

No pre-treatment control or design feature in the inventory measures perceived fairness or justice, or serves as a reasonable proxy for it. c8 (trust in political parties) is related to perceived legitimacy but is not a fairness measure or proxy, and it is classified as an intervening_variable, so it cannot count as adjustment. The other controls do not capture fairness perceptions.

No pre-treatment control in the inventory covers personality as a broad set of stable dispositions. Education (c10) measures educational attainment and may proxy political knowledge or cognitive skills, but it is not a substantively reasonable proxy for personality traits generally. The other controls do not cover this confounder; no structural argument removes it.

No inventory entry directly controls policy exposure, and none is a substantively reasonable proxy for whether respondents are subject to, eligible for, assigned to, or directly affected by a law, program, or rule. c13 controls area of residence, which captures settlement and local context rather than policy exposure; c9 measures election importance, not policy exposure. The other controls do not cover this construct. Therefore, no control or design feature addresses this confounder.

The focal specification does not control for broad political ideology or value orientation, and none of the inventory entries is a reasonable proxy for it. Party membership (c7) measures formal affiliation and involvement, not ideology itself; education (c10) proxies knowledge and cognitive skills, not political orientation. Trust in political parties (c8) is an intervening variable, not a pre-treatment control, and does not measure ideology. No structural argument in the paper removes this confounder.

No inventory entry controls objective political or legal institutional context, or a substantively reasonable proxy for it. The party-organization controls (c1–c6) measure local activity or organizational strength, not the broader institutional environment; the remaining controls measure membership, election importance, demographics, income, or residence. Area of residence (c13) does not adjust for institutional variation. No structural argument in the paper removes this confounder.

The full OLS specification has no control for religious affiliation, religiosity, belief, or practice, and no inventory entry is a substantively reasonable proxy for those concepts. Education (c10) proxies knowledge and cognitive skills, not religion; area of residence (c13) captures local context, not religious belief or practice. Party activity (c1) does not proxy an individual’s religiosity. Trust in parties (c8) is an intervening variable and would not count as a confounder control in any case.

No main-specification control directly measures or reasonably proxies the respondent’s general subjective well-being. The party-activity and organizational-strength measures concern parties and local contact opportunities, not the respondent’s life satisfaction or flourishing; the demographic and election-importance controls do not provide a substantively reasonable proxy. Trust in political parties (c8) is an intervening variable and does not count as a confounder control. No structural argument in the paper removes subjective well-being as a confounder.

No main-specification inventory entry controls for or reasonably proxies substance use. Education (c10), age (c11), income (c12), and the party-related controls do not track respondents’ alcohol, tobacco, or other drug use. Trust in political parties (c8) is an intervening variable and does not count as a control in any case.

No inventory entry covers actual technology use, access, adoption, or frequency of digital-service engagement, directly or as a reasonable proxy. In particular, c8 concerns trust in parties and is an intervening variable, not a control for technology use. No qualifying control or design feature addresses this confounder.

No control-inventory entry covers violence, abuse, or harassment exposure, and none of the listed controls is a reasonable proxy for it. The full model controls for party-related measures and stated demographic or electoral variables, but those do not adjust for violence exposure.

No pre-treatment control or design feature in the inventory covers work characteristics. The controls for party activity, organizational strength, membership, election importance, education, age, income, and residence do not measure or serve as reasonable proxies for job or workplace attributes such as demands, autonomy, schedules, climate, or employment conditions. In particular, income is not a proxy for those characteristics. Trust in parties (c8) is an intervening variable and would not count as confounder adjustment in any event.
